FEEDBACK-GATED MODULATION SUPPORTS VISUAL NAVIGATION

Jingcheng Shi

GitHub

We compare EmbCLIP with EmbCLIP-GaWF on unseen RoboTHOR environments. Both agents receive RGB images and a target object category.

Method

We retain EmbCLIP’s frozen CLIP visual encoder and goal-conditioned processing, and replace its GRU with a parameter-matched GaWF module. The previous step’s detached policy logits feed GaWF’s gates, which modulate its input and recurrent weights.

Results

I. Performance

With lightweight 5M-step training (about 2.5% of EmbCLIP’s original 200M-step budget), EmbCLIP-GaWF achieves higher validation SR and SPL than EmbCLIP.

5M-frame training. Mean ± SD across five runs per model on 1,783 shared validation episodes. The 200M Test result is reported in the original paper, Table 1; it is a separate split and protocol.

II. Recurrent Feedback Guides Navigation Toward the Object Goal

We compare the agents on matched Object Goal Navigation tasks. Both reach GarbageCan and SprayBottle, with EmbCLIP-GaWF finishing sooner. The selected Bowl and HousePlant episodes also show EmbCLIP failures under the lightweight training budget.

Paired trajectories and synchronized first-person views share the same episode, starting pose and random seeds. Grad-CAM below uses separate successful episodes.

III. Grad-CAM Reveals Visual Cues Behind the Stopping Decision

We analyze the trained agents with Grad-CAM to inspect visual information associated with stopping. The selected successful terminal views show each model’s sensitivity when the target is visible. These are separate episodes, not the terminal frames of the videos.

Grad-CAM at successful stops, using each model’s own view and history. Colors are normalized per map; warm regions indicate positive contribution to stopping. Baseball Bat uses different episodes.
